list.listitem: Consider a diagnosis of rosacea in adults over 30 years of age with fixed centrofacial erythema with periods of intensification or with phymatous changes. Diagnosis can also be made by the presence of two or more major features, which include flushing, papules and pustules, telangiectasia, and ocular manifestations. C

Effective phenotype-based first-line treatments include topical α-adrenergic agonists for persistent erythema; topical ivermectin, topical azelaic acid, topical metronidazole, topical minocycline, and oral tetracyclines for papules and pustules; and oral omega-3 fatty acids and cyclosporine ophthalmic emulsion for ocular manifestations. A

Effective phenotype-based second-line treatments include daily oral paroxetine for refractory erythema; B laser and light-based therapies for telangiectasia and persistent erythema; systemic isotretinoin for moderate to severe papules and pustules; and oral doxycycline for ocular manifestations. A
Avoid topical clindamycin, with or without tretinoin, as it appears no better than placebo. A
Combination topical, systemic, and surgical therapies may benefit patients with severe rosacea or those with multiple phenotypes. B

background.definition: Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory cutaneous syndrome of the central face, including the cheeks, nose, chin, and central forehead, characterized by exacerbations and remissions. Common symptoms include facial flushing, erythema, telangiectasia, edema, papules, pustules, ocular lesions, and rhinophyma.

list.listitem: An observational study showed incidence rate of 1.65 per 1000 person-years in the UK.
Onset generally in age >30, most prevalent age 45-60.
More commonly identified in women, but the limited epidemiologic studies show no statistical difference between men and women.
Meta-analysis estimates global prevalence of approximately 5.46% of adults. In whites, it may be >10%.
Symptoms may cause low self-esteem, embarrassment, frustration, social isolation, and even depression.
Genetic and environmental factors can trigger initiation and aggravation of condition.
Emotional stress, alcohol, sun exposure (UV radiation), spicy food, exercise, microorganisms, skin care products and cosmetics may be triggering factors, but are not causative.

Unknown. However, newer evidence suggests that rosacea's different features may be part of a continuum of inflammation that may not be clinically visible but can be detected histologically and biochemically. Current research supports the idea that common flushing and erythema may lead to papules, pustules, and possibly phymas.
One new study suggests the signaling neuropeptide PACAP, a regulator of flushing and edema, are upregulated in rosacea.

Trigger factors can lead to dysregulation of the innate and adaptive immune system; lead to release of mediators like keratinocytes, endothelial cells, mast cells, macrophages, and T helper cells; and can directly communicate to the cutaneous nervous system (neurovascular and neuro-immune active neuropeptides).

Microorganisms are thought to be a factor, but exact role is unclear. Demodex spp, H. pylori, and other microorganisms have been associated with rosacea in some studies, but other studies and reviews have not shown direct links or improvement in rosacea symptoms after treatment.

Consider a diagnosis of rosacea in adults over 30 years of age with fixed centrofacial erythema with periods of intensification or with phymatous changes. Diagnosis can also be made by the presence of two or more major features, which include flushing, papules and pustules, telangiectasia, and ocular manifestations. C
Since diagnosis is clinical, biopsy is generally not required. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Facial rash, no papules or pustules, systemic complaints
Papules, vesicles, or pustules around mouth, nose, or periorbital; children and adults
History of topical steroid use on the face
Pustules around hair follicle, honey crusts
Fungal infection, beard area, scaling, circular, positive KOH prep
Rapid onset of papules, pustules, nodules with fluctuance in young women

list.listitem: Rosacea is a clinical diagnosis. See for phenotypes and diagnostic criteria. Diagnosis requires at least 1 diagnostic or 2 major features.
Rosacea may include one or more of the following secondary features: burning or stinging, dry appearance, edema, ocular manifestations.
Rosacea often reveals an adult with red skin of the face with or without prominent blood vessels, papules, pustules, enlarged lumpy nose and inflammation of the eyes.

Many patients will state that their condition worsens with sun exposure, hot temperature, hot spicy food, and alcohol. Many have fair skin and a family history of rosacea, and many patients may blush or flush easily.

Classify patients based on their phenotype: erythematotelangiectatic/vascular, papulopustular/inflammatory, ocular, phymatous, as well as based on the presence of telagectasias, dryness, ocular involvement, pustules, or dry skin.
Rosacea is a clinical diagnosis.

Skin biopsy findings are usually nonspecific and therefore rarely indicated. Occasionally when the diagnosis is not clear, a shave or punch biopsy can provide histology to make the diagnosis or rule out other diagnoses.
Once the clinical diagnosis is made, phenotype-based treatment can be initiated using this rosacea treatment algorithm ().

Effective phenotype-based first-line treatments include topical α-adrenergic agonists for persistent erythema; topical ivermectin, topical azelaic acid, topical metronidazole, topical minocycline, and oral tetracyclines for papules and pustules; and oral omega-3 fatty acids and cyclosporine ophthalmic emulsion for ocular manifestations. A

Effective phenotype-based second-line treatments include daily oral paroxetine for refractory erythema; B laser and light-based therapies for telangiectasia and persistent erythema; systemic isotretinoin for moderate to severe papules and pustules; and oral doxycycline for ocular manifestations. A
Combination topical, systemic, and surgical therapies may benefit patients with severe rosacea or those with multiple phenotypes. B

For the temporary treatment of persistent erythema, the α-adrenergic agonists brimonidine 0.33% gel and oxymetazoline 1% cream induce transient vasoconstriction reducing facial erythema within 30 minute of application, reaching a peak in 3-6 hours. In four studies, both agents showed improvement in patient self-assessment compared to placebo. (brimonidine RR 2.11, 95% CI 1.60-2.78, NNT 5; oxymetazoline RR 1.65, 95% CI 1.23-2.21, NNT 11). Both agents were well tolerated with erythema, pruritus, irritation, flushing, and headache most frequently reported.

For the treatment of mild to moderate papules and pustules, azelaic acid 15% gel, 20% cream, or 15% foam twice daily (6 studies, n = 2,223); topical ivermectin 1% cream once daily (2 studies, n = 1,371); topical metronidazole 0.75% gel or 1% cream twice daily (9 studies, n = 2,107); and minocycline 1.5% or 3% foam once daily (1 study, n = 232) are superior in participant-assessed improvements and lesion counts compared to placebo.

Topical ivermectin appears to be more effective than topical metronidazole, based on one study (n = 962), when measuring patient-assessed improvements (RR 1.14, 95% CI 1.07-1.22 (P <0.001); NNT 10) with no difference in adverse events. Similarly, topical ivermectin was slighty more effective than topical metronidazole for improving quality of life (QOL) and physician-assessed outcomes. In contrast, three studies (n = 451) showed conflicting findings on efficacy and adverse events when comparing topical azelaic acid and topical metronidazole, hence no firm conclusions can be made.

For rosacea with combined features of erythema and papulopustules, combination topical therapy with brimonidine 0.33% gel in the morning and ivermectin 1% cream at night appears better than placebo (vehicle), based on patient- and physician-assessed outcomes in one study (n = 190).
Topical clindamycin, with or without tretinoin, was no better than placebo in three studies (n = 629).

Other topical treatments, including permethrin, dapsone, sodium sulfacetamide with sulfur, pimecrolimus, tranexamic acid, praziquantel, diclofenac sodium, manuka honey, and botulinum toxin (injections), have unclear or limited data to support their use.

Topical treatment for mild to moderate papules and pustules can be maintained once desired results are achieved. Data from 3 RCTs support the efficacy and safety of topical ivermectin 1% cream, acelaic acid 15% gel, and metronidazole 0.75% gel for maintenance therapy. If no improvement is achieved in 8-12 weeks, consider adding systemic therapy (see below).

For the treatment of ocular features, low-certainty evidence from one study (n = 37) showed the superiority of cyclosporine ophthalmic emulsion 0.05% twice daily for 3 months over artificial tears in improving QOL and physician-assessed tear production (Schirmer test); adverse events were similar between the two groups. Another study (n = 38) compared cyclosporine ophthalmic emulsion twice daily for 3 months and oral doxycycline 100mg twice daily for 1 month (then tapered to once daily for 2 months) and showed low-certainty evidence that cyclosporine ophthalmic was better at improving QOL, physician- and patient-assessed outcomes.

For the treatment of moderate to severe papules and pustules, combined topical and systemic therapy is recommended. One study (n = 72) showed the superiority of combined oral doxycycline 40mg modified release (MR) and topical metronidazole over monotherapy with topical metronidazole for treating papules and pustules, with added benefits for erythema. However, addition of topical azelaic acid to minocycline 45mg daily did not improve its efficacy, based on one study deemed as low-certainty evidence.

Doxycycline 40mg MR once daily, based on two studies (n = 707) was superior to placebo in achieving physician-assessed "clear or almost clear" status (RR 1.69, 95% CI 1.26-2.28; P <0.001; NNT 9), based on high-certainty evidence. Additionally, doxycycline 40mg MR daily reduced erythema more than placebo, based on three studies deemed as moderate-certainty evidence. Doxycycline 40mg MR appears comparable to doxycycline 100mg but with less adverse effects, based on one study (n = 91) deemed as low-certainty evidence. Unfortunately, doxycycline 40mg MR is more expensive than generic doxycycline 100 mg.

Minocycline 100mg daily appears to be noninferior to doxycycline 40mg MR daily based on one study (n = 80) deemed as low-certainty evidence. However, the 2021 British Association of Dermatologists (BAD) guidelines recommend avoiding oral minocycline for patients with rosacea given the increased risk for adverse effects, unless no other treatment options are available.

A double-blinded RCT enrolling 653 adults with moderate to severe rosacea found the new formulation of minocycline (10 mg immediate release + 30 mg delayed release) to be more effective than doxycyline 40 mg after 16 weeks of treatment, based on the investigator's global assessment (IGA), with NNT = 3 to 5. This new minocycline formulation is expensive ($1,200 per month on GoodRx on 8/26/25).

Oral tetracycline 250 mg twice daily, based on two studies (n = 151) lasting only 4 and 6 weeks, was better than placebo in improving physician-assessed but not patient-assessed lesion count (low-certainty evidence).
Based on very low-certainty evidence from one study (n = 67), azithromycin 500mg three times a week (then tapered) appears comparable to doxycycline 100mg daily in terms of efficacy and safety.

Over a period of 8-12 weeks, if moderate to severe papules and pustules are improving, oral antibiotics can be maintained for up to 12-16 weeks, then consider tapering systemic antibiotics while maintaining the patient on topical therapy.
Over a period of 8-12 weeks, if moderate to severe papules and pustules are not improving with oral antibiotics, consider switching to systemic isotretinoin.

Systemic treatment with low-dose isotretinoin 0.25 mg/kg for 4 months is superior to placebo in the treatment of refractory or frequently relapsing papulopustular rosacea, based on one study (n = 156). Based on high-certainty evidence, isotretinoin was much better than placebo in reaching a 90% reduction in inflammatory lesions (RR 5.51, 95% CI 2.37-12.83; P <0.001; NNT 2). However, more adverse events occurred with isotretinoin, including xerosis, eczema, cheilitis, myalgia, arthralgia, abdominal pain, and dry eyes (RR 1.59, 95% CI 1.12-2.24; P<0.009; NNTH 4).

Low-dose isotretinoin 0.3 mg/kg appears to be slightly more effective than doxycycline 100 mg daily for 14 days (then tapered to 50mg daily) for treating severe papules and pustules based on one study (n = 261); adverse events appear comparable between the two groups.

Over a period of 12-16 weeks, if moderate to severe papules and pustules are improving with low-dose isotretinoin, consider discontinuing isotretinoin while maintaining the patient on topical therapy. Extra precautions are needed to prevent pregnancy in women of child-bearing age who require isotretinoin therapy.
For clinically inflammed phyma, experts recommend doxycycline and isotretenoin but no RCTs are available to support this.
Patients experiencing predominantly transient facial erythema (flushing) may benefit from oral propranolol.

Treatment refractory erythema can be treated with oral paroxetine 25mg daily, based on a prospective RCT of 112 patients that found paroxetine superior to placebo at 12 weeks in reducing erythema (using Clinical Erythema Assessment [CEA] score, 42.9% vs 20.8%; NNT = 5.7; 95% CI 3.0 - 93.2). Flushing and burning sensation were also improved compared to placebo (44.9% vs 25% and 46.9% vs 18.8%, respectively), but not telangiectasia, lesion counts, and rosacea quality-of-life score.

Anti-calcitonin gene related peptide (CGRP) receptor monoclonal antibodies are being studied in the treatment of rosacea. One small, non-randomized controlled trial of 30 patients showed possible benefit of subcutaneous erenumab when given every 4 weeks over a period of 12 weeks. Moderate to extreme flushing was reduced by an average of -6.9 days (95% CI, -10.4 to -3.4 days; P < .001) from 23.6 (5.8) days at baseline. Moderate to severe erythema was reduced by an average -8.1 days (95% CI, -12.5 to -3.7 days; P < .001) from 15.2 (9.1) days at baseline. However, larger randomized trials are needed.

For the treatment of ocular features, moderate-certainty evidence from one study (n = 130) found omega-3 fatty acids (180mg eicosapentaenoic acid and 120mg docosahexaenoic acid) twice daily superior to placebo in improving dry eyes from rosacea as assessed by patients and physicians.

For the treatment of telangiectasia and erythema, low- to moderate-certainty evidence from a few small RCTs (n = 16-49) support the efficacy of pulsed dye laser (PDL), neodymium-doped yttrium aluminum garnet (Nd:YAG) laser, and intense pulsed light therapy.

For clinically noninflamed phyma, experts recommend surgical therapies, including electrodessication, ablative surgery, and laser therapy. However, no RCTs have been published to support this recommendation.

One RCT (n = 44) showed that 3-5 sessions of 5-Aminolevulinic acid photodynamic therapy (ALA-PDT) may be non-inferior to oral minocycline (100 mg daily) at reducing papulopustular lesions and improving rosacea-specific quality of life. However, improvement in the CEA score with ALA-PDT was inferior to that of minocycline (35% vs 67%).
Avoid triggers such as sun exposure, hot drinks, spicy food, and alcohol which can vary from patient to patient.
Avoid sun exposure and wear a hat and sunscreen when outdoors during the day.
Don't rub or abrade the skin on the face; this worsens rosacea.
Avoid products that irritate skin or cause burning or stinging and avoid comedogenic products on the face.
Food triggers are not universal, so patients should avoid foods that they determine worsen their own rosacea; these may include hot and spicy foods.

Beverages, like alcohol and hot drinks, may be triggers. A prospective cohort study studied 82,737 women and compared to non-drinkers found increased alcohol intake was significantly associated with elevated risk of rosacea in a linear dose-dependent link with alcohol (hazard ratio (HR) = 1.12, 95% CI 1.05-1.2 for alcohol intake 1-4 g/day; HR = 1.19, 95% CI 1.08-1.31 for 5-9 g/day; HR = 1.37, 1.2-1.56 for 15-29 g/day). A 4-ounce glass of wine or 1-ounce glass of liquor is equal to 12 g of alcohol. Specifically, white wine and liquor were associated with a significant increased risk of rosacea and red wine and beer were not.
For ocular rosacea, avoid cosmetics and environments involving dry or smoky air.
If rosacea is temperature related, avoid saunas, hot tubs, hot baths, and hot showers.
If rosacea is weather related, avoid sun, wind, and cold.
Refer patients with moderate to severe ocular disease to ophthalmology, especially if treatment with cyclosporine emulsion or systemic doxycycline is being considered.
Experts recommend ophthalmology referral for corneal involvment, sudden eye pain, visual decline, or suspected ocular disease in children.
Refer patients to appropriate surgeon if the patient chooses surgical treatment of rhinophyma.
The signs and symptoms of rosacea can be improved with many treatments. A
Among rosacea's major features, telangiectasia is most resistant to treatment. A

For pregnant and lactating women, consider topical metronidazole or azelaic acid. If no improvement is seen and patient desires step-up therapy, consider combining topical therapy with oral azithromycin.
Topical and systemic retinoids should be avoided in pregancy.

For ocular manifestations in pregnant and lactating women, start with artificial tears and eyelid hygiene. If response is insufficient, consider topical fusidic acid or refer to ophthalmologist for consideration for cyclosporine ophthalmic emulsion.
Rosacea is uncommon in the pediatric population.

For the treatment of papules and pustules in children, experts recommend topical metronidazole or azelaic acid. If response is insufficient and patient and/or parents desire step-up therapy, consider oral metronidazole or tetracycline (only for children >8 years-old).
Though uncommon in children, ocular features present more frequently than cutaneous manifestations, and often, more severely.

feature.caption: Phenotypes of Rosacea.
feature.feature_body:
Diagnostic* Major† Secondary
Fixed centrofacial erythema in a characteristic pattern that may periodically intensify • Phymatous changes Flushing papules and pustules • Telangiectasia • Ocular manifestations • Lid margin telangiectasia • Interpalpebral conjunctival injection • Spade-shaped infiltrates in the cornea • Scleritis and sclerokeratitis Burning sensation • Stinging sensation • Edema • Dryness • Ocular manifestations • “Honey crust” and collarette accumulation at the base of the lashes • Irregularity of the lid margin • Evaporative tear dysfunction (rapid tear breakup time)
*These features by themselves are diagnostic of rosacea†Two or more major features may be considered diagnostic
